description: We're Shah and Kai, two Macquarie University students with experience in cybersecurity, web prototyping and hackathons. We're building an offline health check-in tool for astronauts to track sleep and activity and share a summary when contact with Mission Control returns. We'd love to team up with someone interested in health science, UI/UX or data visualisation. If you like turning ideas into working demos, come build with us!
summary: When contact with Earth is delayed, astronauts still need to spot changes in their health and decide what to do. Pulsar is an offline prototype that helps them log readings such as blood pressure, resting heart rate, blood glucose, temperature, sleep and mood. It compares readings with the astronaut’s own baseline, explains flagged changes and offers a checklist of follow-up steps. When communications resume, the crew can export a digitally signed handover for Mission Control to verify. Pulsar addresses the challenge’s gather, evaluate and act workflow. We tested it using synthetic health readings from simulated missions.
details:
Pulsar helps astronauts assess their health during communications delays and blackouts. Crew members log the six indicators named in the challenge along with food intake, exercise, resistance training, body mass, stress, social contact and symptoms. The mission routine shows which checks are due. NASA’s Human Research Program informed the health areas, and the ISS Reaction Self Test inspired the optional reaction-time check.

Pulsar uses an exponentially weighted moving average to detect changes against a rolling personal baseline. The Today screen explains the top alert and highlights affected health areas on a clickable astronaut. Trends show how readings change over time, and missing readings are marked explicitly. Each alert includes a checklist, and completed steps stay attached to the alert. The Guide explains how to take measurements in flight. Mission settings provide gravity and communications context for the ISS, Moon, Mars transit and Mars surface.

Readings stay on the device with optional passphrase encryption. The crew can export a signed summary of alerts, trends and completed actions. Mission Control verifies it against a previously registered crew key. Our Day 51 demo shows the crew responding to a simulated fever during a blackout, then demonstrates verification of the signed handover and rejection of a tampered copy.

We built Pulsar with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, IndexedDB and Web Crypto. A service worker enables offline use after the first load. Node.js supported validation, and Chromium and FFmpeg supported demo production. Pulsar flagged all four scripted events in the 180-day demo mission, averaging one day from event onset. Across 50 additional synthetic missions, it flagged 200 of 200 scripted events with 0.36 false-alarm episodes per 30 days. These results describe performance in our simulator.

Anthropic Claude Code assisted with Pulsar’s code, synthetic mission generator, testing and documentation. ChatGPT assisted with brainstorming, development and testing for the CrewRelay prototype used in the opening, and with reviewing the submission. OpenAI image generation created the lunar backdrop, and Higgsfield (ByteDance Seed Audio) generated narration from our team’s script. The demo labels both the backdrop and the narration.
